children: Semiconductor powerhouse Taiwan is confident that it will keep its existing 15% tariff rate from the United States, the government said on Thursday after US President Donald Trump fired a new tariff salvo on 14 major trading partners.

The Trump administration proposed new maximum potential rates of 20% to 40% to counter excess industrial capacity that ‌it says these countries are promoting. In February, the US Supreme Court struck down previous global tariffs.
But the US Trade Representative's office said it intends to cap new tariffs at lower levels agreed under trade deals that are completed or still under negotiation.

Taiwan and the US signed an investment cooperation Memorandum of Understanding and an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, or ART, in January and February of this year, which secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other tech products, which account for over 70% of Taiwan's exports to the US.
Based on communications between Taipei and Washington, Taiwan's government said it is confident that both sides will maintain the previously agreed-upon 15%.

"The US has one main goal, which is to rebuild the legal basis for its reciprocal tariff policy. It is not to change the content of the agreements themselves," Taiwan Vice Premier Cheng Li-chiun, who has led trade talks with Washington, told reporters.
"Both sides have repeatedly said they hope to maintain the content of the agreements. So the agreement as a whole will not change and will not be renegotiated," she added.
Separate Section 232 tariffs on semiconductors and their derivatives have not yet been announced, but Taiwan has already secured most-favoured treatment in advance through the MOU, Cheng said.

Under January's deal with the US, Taiwanese companies will invest $250 billion to boost production of semiconductors, energy and artificial intelligence in the US, while Taiwan will also guarantee an additional $250 billion in credit to facilitate further investment.
Taiwan is also investing $4.4 billion in a new liquefied natural gas project in Alaska that Trump has championed, though details remain to be ironed out.
Speaking at the same news conference with Cheng, Economy Minister Kung Ming-hsin said the Alaska plan was a necessity for Taiwan.

"Because part of our long-term contracts are with Qatar, where the risk is relatively higher, so we hope to move part of those long-term contracts to the US to reduce that risk and improve the resilience of our energy sources," Kung said.
